content.title: HABITS THAT SEEM HEALTHY BUT ARE QUIETLY {{BACKFIRING}}
facts: **Drinking a gallon of water a day** -> can flush out sodium and potassium faster than you replace them, leaving you tired and crampy even though you're 'hydrated'.
**Running on an empty stomach every morning** -> pushes your body to break down muscle tissue for fuel once glycogen stores run low, especially on longer sessions.
**Sleeping with a heavy weighted blanket every night** -> can trap body heat and disrupt the natural temperature drop your body needs to reach deep sleep.
**Snacking on granola bars as a 'healthy' choice** -> often delivers as much sugar as a candy bar, just wrapped in oats and dried fruit.
**Doing an intense workout right before bed** -> spikes cortisol and heart rate at the exact time your body should be winding down, delaying sleep onset.
**Taking a daily multivitamin 'just in case'** -> can lead to excess fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) building up in your tissues over time instead of simply being excreted.
**Stretching cold muscles before a workout** -> can actually reduce power output and increase strain, since static stretching temporarily loosens the tendon's spring-like response.
**Sipping herbal tea all day instead of water** -> some blends act as mild diuretics, meaning you could be losing more fluid than you're taking in.

content.caption:
A few of these deserve a closer look. Take the gallon-a-day **water** habit — when you flood your system with plain water and no electrolytes, your kidneys work overtime to dilute and excrete it, taking sodium and potassium along for the ride, which is why some big water-drinkers still feel foggy or crampy. Then there's the **granola bar**: many are made with inverted syrups and dried fruit concentrates that spike blood sugar almost as fast as a dessert, even though the packaging screams 'wholesome'. And that **multivitamin** you take out of habit? Because vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble, your body stores the extra instead of flushing it out like it does with vitamin C, so daily 'insurance' doses can quietly accumulate. Everyone's body and diet are different, so it's worth checking what actually applies to yours.
